tier_reason: Public harness (cbench in nordlow/compiler-benchmark; ./benchmark is a symlink to it) with every compiler command line in code (gcc/clang/g++/clang++ get only -Wall -Wextra plus -fsyntax-only, -c or -o, i.e. default -O0; dmd gets -betterC and, for build, -Xcc=-fuse-ld=lld when ld.lld is present), compiler versions in the README table and the CPU named (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 at 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux, 2026-09 run), so it meets A; upgraded from B because the flags the record could not read are in the public script.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (Ryzen AI 7 350, 2026-09): D (dmd 2.113.0) Total=Build+Run 13 us/f untemplated (19 templated), Compile 10.3 us/f (17.9 templated), Check 4.5 us/f, against C (clang 23.1.1) Total 118 us/f and Compile 77.9, C++ (clang++ 23.1.1) Total 236 (107 templated) and Compile 82.4 (128.7), C++ (g++-15 15.3.0) Total 303 (600) and Compile 269.6 (665.0), C (gcc-15 15.3.0) Total 392 and Compile 193.8, C (gcc 16.2.1) Total 454, C++ (g++ 16.2.1) Total 486. About 9x faster than clang C and 23x faster than g++-15 on Total, and about 7.6x (clang C) to 26x (g++-15) on the link-free Compile column (derived from page data). The README's '6x-38x' headline is dmd against the other D compilers (ldmd2 1.43.0 Total 95 us/f, gdc 16.2.1 Total 527 us/f), not against C. The C compiler tcc 0.9.28rc is faster than dmd (Total 4 us/f, Compile 2.0 us/f).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: From cbench: C/C++ via gcc, g++, clang, clang++ with -Wall -Wextra (C) or -Wno-c++11-extensions (C++) and no -O flag (default -O0); check uses -fsyntax-only, compile uses -c, build links with the compiler's default system linker. dmd and ldmd2 use -betterC; check -o-, compile -c, build adds -Xcc=-fuse-ld=lld (or gold) when available; gdc gets no extra flags. Versions: dmd 2.113.0-95551bb, ldmd2 1.43.0, gdc 16.2.1, clang/clang++ 23.1.1, gcc/g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1. Minimum of --run-count=10 repetitions (capped to 3 or 2 for slow steps), workers pinned to cores in a multiprocessing pool.
corrections.caveats: Compile-time claim, not run-time: both sides build unoptimized code (gcc/clang default -O0, dmd without -O), so the -O3 rule for run-time baselines does not apply. Not a language-level win: the C compiler tcc compiles the same generated program faster than dmd (Total 4 vs 13 us/f) and cuik and cproc are close (76 and 86 us/f), so the gap is dmd's implementation against GCC and Clang, as the dmd vs ldmd2 vs gdc rows show. Harness asymmetries: D builds link with lld via -Xcc=-fuse-ld=lld while gcc and clang use the default system linker, and D uses -betterC (no druntime), which favours D in the Total=Build+Run column; the link-free Compile column still shows 7.6x to 26x. C adds -Wall -Wextra. Synthetic arithmetic call chains in one translation unit, no headers, standard library or modules; the README says real builds differ. Noisy cells: clang++ templated Total 107 is below its own Compile 128.7, and clang++ untemplated Total 236 is nearly 3x its Compile 82.4; the README prose (dmd 11.5, ldmd2 70.3, gdc 433.2, clang 87 us/f) comes from a different run than the tables. Single machine, single sample run by a D community developer (nordlow).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars (dlang/dmd); benchmark repo nordlow/compiler-benchmark 167 stars, 17 forks, MIT
corrections.why_faster: dmd's own front end and lightly optimizing custom backend generate code quickly; the same D source through LLVM (ldmd2, 95 us/f) or GCC (gdc, 527 us/f) is much slower, so the speed is the toolchain's, not the language's. D also links with lld and -betterC in the harness while gcc and clang use the default linker.

notes: Numbers match the README table exactly; flags read from the cbench script (the 'benchmark' file is a 6-byte symlink to cbench, which is why the search agent got a 6-byte body). Record as a toolchain compile-speed entry rather than a D-beats-C language claim: tcc (C) is faster than dmd on the same benchmark, and the D build uses lld while C/C++ builds use the default linker. The orchestrator may want a compile-time or toolchain category instead of systems-and-safety.

tier_reason: The C2Rust result (91 cycles, 121 instructions per packet) is a two-sentence addendum the authors added to Rust-vs-C-performance.md on 2019-10-30 (commit e543831, 'rust can be faster than C :)'), after the ANCS 2019 paper; the transpiled code, compiler versions and flags are not published, so it is first-party numbers without methodology (C), not peer-reviewed (B).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Rust-vs-C-performance.md: the C2Rust-transpiled, fully unsafe Rust driver forwards a packet in 91 cycles with 121 instructions, 'faster than the original code', also when C is compiled with clang on the same LLVM version. The C rows in the same document are 94 cycles and 127 instructions at batch 32 (108 and 139 at batch 8), so about 3% fewer cycles than C at batch 32 (derived from page data; the document does not state the batch size of the C2Rust run). The idiomatic safe Rust driver is slower: 100 vs 94 cycles at batch 32 and 120 vs 108 at batch 8, executing 65% more instructions.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C baseline: emmericp/ixy CMakeLists.txt compiles with -g -O2 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer (current HEAD; the file was last changed in November 2019). ixy.rs Cargo.toml sets no profile overrides (cargo release default opt-level 3, no target-cpu). Compiler versions and the C2Rust build's flags are not stated.
corrections.caveats: The C2Rust claim is a tongue-in-cheek addendum added to the repository on 2019-10-30, after the ANCS 2019 paper; whether the paper contains it could not be checked (arXiv and net.in.tum.de blocked here). The transpiled C2Rust driver is not published in the ixy-languages organisation as far as I could find. The difference is 3 cycles per packet from one run on one Intel Xeon E3-1230 v3, with no variance reported, and the batch size of the C2Rust run is not stated. The C baseline is built at -O2 -march=native, not -O3, while Rust release builds default to opt-level 3, so optimisation levels are not matched. The document gives no mechanism beyond 6 fewer instructions per packet. Hardware differs between this document (E3-1230 v3) and the README throughput graphs (E3-1230 v2). The repository has been quiet since December 2022; the README marks each driver 'Finished'.
corrections.why_faster: Not explained by the source: the transpiled unsafe Rust executes 121 instead of 127 instructions per packet (a different LLVM pipeline from rustc at its default opt-level against C at -O2); for safe Rust the document says out-of-order CPUs hide bounds-check overhead (IPC 2.09 vs 1.35), which is why it is only 6-11% slower.

notes: Numbers are on the page but the 'Rust is faster than C' line rests on a 3-cycle difference from unpublished transpiled code, added after the paper; tier C. The C baseline is -O2 (emmericp/ixy CMakeLists.txt), so it misses the wave's -O3 rule; record shortcomings: unmatched opt levels, no published C2Rust code, no flags or versions, single run, within-noise gain.

tier_reason: The README table gives first-party run times with no hardware, tool versions, commands or benchmark script; the Bioinformatics 2018 paper is peer-reviewed and a search snippet confirms it compares against samtools depth, BEDTools genomecov and Sambamba, but its numbers could not be opened (OUP, PMC and bioRxiv blocked), and wave-14 rules keep snippet-only paper evidence at C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Nim with --mm:refc (nim.cfg) and -d:release; nim.cfg comment: nim c -a -d:static -d:release mosdepth.nim with htslib configured --with-libdeflate --disable-libcurl. Nim's release build passes -O3 -fno-ident -fno-math-errno to gcc (nim-lang/Nim config/nim.cfg gcc.options.speed). samtools' default Makefile uses CFLAGS -g -Wall -O2; the flags of the samtools, bedtools and sambamba builds actually timed are not stated.
corrections.caveats: The README table lists no hardware, tool versions or commands; tier B would rest on the Bioinformatics 2018 paper, which was not opened (publisher, PMC and bioRxiv blocked; a search snippet confirms the comparison but gives no numbers). Results date from 2017 samtools and htslib. Both mosdepth and samtools decode BAM/CRAM with htslib (C); mosdepth's documented build links htslib with libdeflate, and the htslib build used by samtools in the table is not stated, so part of the gap may be decompression rather than mosdepth's code. By default mosdepth corrects mate overlaps and walks CIGAR operations; --fast-mode (-x) skips both; the README does not say which mode the timing table used, and its accuracy check compared samtools depth defaults with mosdepth without overlap detection. The speedup is algorithmic (difference array against samtools' pileup), not a Nim-versus-C effect; mosdepth uses far more memory (1196 MB vs 27 MB for samtools). Opt levels are not matched if default builds were used (Nim release -O3, samtools Makefile -O2).

notes: Numbers match the README table exactly (BAM samtools 50:12 vs mosdepth 25:23, relative 1.98; CRAM 1.79; sambamba 5.71; bedtools 5.31; 3-thread window 8:44). Downgraded to C because the only openable evidence is first-party and lacks methodology; the record's caveat that mosdepth skips mate-overlap correction by default was wrong and is corrected. Notable (878 stars, widely cited Bioinformatics paper, bioconda); keep as a project entry with language_level_claim false.
